title: Noble rot and Sauternes
subtitle: Sémillon's sweet glory
objectives: Explain how noble rot affects Sémillon

steps.title: The Ciron's mist
steps.body: In Sauternes and Barsac, the cool Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne, creating autumn mists. Morning humidity lets Botrytis cinerea grow; sunny afternoons stop grey rot. On Sémillon's thin skins, the fungus shrivels berries, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour, and adding honey, apricot and marmalade.

steps.title: Sauternes
steps.body: Pickers pass through the vineyard several times, called tries, choosing only botrytised berries. Yields can be tiny, a glass of wine per vine at Château d'Yquem. Wines are fermented and aged in oak for up to three years, reaching about 13 to 14% alcohol and 100 to 150 g/l of sugar.

steps.prompt: Put the making of Sauternes in order.
items: Mist and sun bring noble rot
steps.explanation: Noble rot first, then careful selection, then slow fermentation and ageing.

steps.title: Ageing
steps.body: Sauternes is one of the longest-lived wines. Over decades, it darkens from gold to amber, developing crème brûlée, saffron, dried apricot and marmalade. Good vintages last 50 years or more. Château d'Yquem, the only Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855, is the most famous.

steps.prompt: What is a trie in Sauternes?
options: A pass through the vineyard to pick botrytised berries
steps.explanation: Several tries pick only the berries that are ready.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Ciron's mists bring noble rot to Sémillon
Pickers make several tries; yields are tiny
Sauternes ages for decades, darkening to amber
